claims.text: The transient ductile-brittle-ductile transition in FCC/B2 eutectic HEAs is driven by temperature-dependent evolution of local chemical order within the B2 phase.
Local chemical order in the B2 phase modulates the critical resolved shear stress for dislocation slip in ordered domains.
The transition is not caused by grain-boundary segregation.
The initial alloy has a fine-grained FCC/B2 eutectic microstructure.
The initial alloy has no pre-existing impurity segregation at grain boundaries.
Intermediate thermal aging produces transient brittleness at specific aging temperatures.
The relevant aging regime lies below the threshold for significant grain coarsening.
The relevant aging regime lies below the threshold for classical impurity segregation.
Short-range and local chemical order evolves within the B2 phase during aging.
Evolution of local chemical order leads to the formation of anti-phase boundaries.
The evolving ordered structure transiently raises the energy barrier for dislocation cross-slip or climb.
At intermediate aging temperatures, local chemical ordering in the B2 phase transiently increases.
Increased local chemical ordering raises stacking-fault energy.
Increased local chemical ordering raises anti-phase-boundary energy.
Higher stacking-fault and anti-phase-boundary energies lock dislocations in ordered domains and cause brittle fracture.
At higher aging temperatures, local chemical order decays or transforms into a configuration that offers less resistance to dislocations.
Reduced resistance to dislocation bypass at higher temperatures restores ductility.
The brittleness peak coincides with a peak in local chemical order in the B2 phase.
Grain-boundary chemistry remains unchanged through the brittleness peak.
Classical grain-boundary embrittlement models attribute brittleness to segregation of impurities such as P, S, or B at grain boundaries.
